text: The previous course taught the real triage loop of fire, review, classify, act as a generic SOC process. Sentinel implements that loop around one specific object: the incident. This lesson covers what an incident actually is, how severity works, and how the Incidents page turns that generic loop into a concrete, repeatable workflow.

An incident is not the same thing as an alert. A single analytics rule, or several related ones, can fire multiple alerts on the same underlying entities — a suspicious sign-in, a new OAuth grant on that account, and a new mail-forwarding rule minutes later. Rather than handing an analyst three disconnected alerts, Sentinel's incident correlation groups them into one incident, so opening it shows the full picture of what happened to one account at once.

Every incident gets a severity, set by the analytics rule that generated it: Informational, Low, Medium, or High. Informational is worth recording but needs no independent action. Low is a little unusual but rarely malicious alone. Medium genuinely warrants a human look, like impossible travel or an unfamiliar admin grant. High closely matches real attack behavior and should jump to the top of the queue regardless of when it arrived.

The Incidents page is the queue itself — a filterable, sortable list showing each incident's severity, status, and owner. The real workflow: filter by severity so High surfaces first, assign the incident to yourself so work isn't duplicated, open it to review the grouped alerts and entities, and move its status from New to Active. Closing it records a verdict — True Positive, False Positive, or Benign Positive — directly on the incident.

Working the queue by severity instead of arrival order is what actually limits dwell time. A Low incident that waited two extra hours cost little; a High incident waiting ten extra minutes could mean ten more minutes of an active attacker operating undetected. Next up: the investigation graph, which maps an incident's entities and how they connect to each other.
